Case Study 02  /  Performance Goals

The flights that got faster without going any faster

A government rule made airline punctuality public. Punctuality improved. The journey did not get shorter. Nearly forty years later the only airline ever fined over it was fined for the opposite thing.

0102030405060708
0%

Everything here is real — a government regulation, named airlines, and figures anyone can look up.

Read it looking for the person who did something wrong. There isn't one. Everybody in this case was competent, and every decision was defensible when it was made.

On 27 December 2025, in the quiet week between Christmas and New Year, American Airlines announced that it was changing how it runs Dallas Fort Worth, the largest hub in its network. Nine daily banks of flights would become thirteen from April. Terminal F would be expanded. And the airline would make what it called a significant investment in block time — the scheduled period between an aircraft pushing back from one gate and reaching another — across flights to and from Dallas and throughout its network.Source 1

Jim Moses, a senior vice president at American, said the operating environment and customer expectations had changed over the previous decade, and that the airline's approach at its largest hub had to change with them.Source 2

The unusual part

Read that announcement carefully and it says something unusual. An airline was telling the public that its flights would be scheduled to take longer, and describing that as an investment in customers.

For most of the previous four decades, the same practice had been the industry's open secret — something airlines did quietly and analysts wrote about with a raised eyebrow. To understand how it became a thing worth announcing, and why the one enforcement action the regulator has ever taken went in the opposite direction, it helps to go back to 1987.

Chapter 01

A number nobody could argue with

In 1987 the United States Department of Transportation began requiring large airlines to report how often their flights arrived on time. The figures were published every month in a consumer report. Anyone could look them up before booking.Source 3

The problem being solved was real. Airline delays were a persistent public complaint, and complaints are hard for a regulator to act on — they arrive one at a time, from people with no way to compare one carrier against another. A published number changes that. If passengers could compare airlines on punctuality, the reasoning went, airlines would compete on it.

The definition had to be simple enough to apply to millions of flights a year. A flight counts as on time if it reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after the arrival time printed in the carrier's reservation system. Fourteen minutes late is on time. Fifteen minutes late is not.Source 4

Image description

A 0 to 30 minute scale with a hard break at 15 minutes. The left band, ON TIME, covers arrivals within 15 minutes of schedule. The right band, LATE, covers arrivals after 15 minutes. A separate green chip for cancelled and diverted flights sits outside the scale entirely, because those flights are not counted either way.

Exhibit 1: The fifteen-minute threshold

ArrivalRecorded as
On scheduleOn time
1 minute lateOn time
14 minutes lateOn time
15 minutes lateLate
3 hours lateLate
CancelledNeither — removed from the calculation
A flight is on time if it reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after the scheduled arrival time. One minute late and fourteen minutes late are recorded identically. Source: Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

Chapter 02

The Department's position

It is worth sitting inside the problem the rule-writers faced, because the choice they made looks obvious only in hindsight.

Whatever they published had to work across every large carrier and every domestic route. It had to be auditable, because airlines would be ranked against each other and a disputed figure is worse than no figure. It had to be understandable by a passenger in the two or three seconds they would spend looking at it. And ideally it would not require a whole new data collection, because the scheduled and actual times already existed in the reservation and reporting systems.

A threshold satisfies all four. It produces one percentage per carrier. It is either met or not, so there is nothing to argue about. A passenger reads eighty-three per cent and knows immediately that it beats seventy-eight. And it can be computed from data the airlines were already recording.

The alternatives are each worse on at least one of those counts. Average minutes late is more informative and much harder to rank fairly, because a handful of extreme delays distort the average and carriers operating in congested airspace would look worse for reasons outside their control. Total journey time says nothing about reliability, which is much of what a nervous traveller is actually buying. Measuring whether passengers reached their final destination the same day is closest to what people care about and would have required tracking individuals across connections, rebookings and other carriers — in 1987, an impossible ask.

The Department did not treat the rule as finished. It was modified in 1995 to include mechanical delays, which the original had left out. In 2000 an advisory committee was formed to consider further changes, and in November 2002 a final rule required airlines to report the causes of delays and cancellations — weather, air traffic control, late-arriving aircraft, security, and the carrier's own operations.Source 3

Both amendments made the picture richer. Neither touched the schedule the flight was measured against.

Decision 1 of 5

Put yourself in 1987

The rule has not been written. Knowing the constraints above, what would you publish?

Chapter 03

What the measure cannot see

Start with what it does well. It is cheap, hard to dispute, and immediately legible. Those three things are why it has survived nearly four decades and is still the definition every ranking uses.

Now look at the edges.

The first gap

The first is the threshold itself. A flight fifteen minutes late and a flight three hours late are recorded identically, and a flight fourteen minutes late is recorded as a success. The measure captures whether a line was crossed, not how long anyone waited.

The second gap

The second gap is larger. Cancelled and diverted flights are counted as neither on time nor late. They leave the calculation entirely and are reported separately.Source 5

That has a consequence which shows up clearly in the 2024 figures. Southwest Airlines finished last of the five largest US carriers on on-time arrivals, at 77.77% — one hundredth of a point behind American. It also completed 99.38% of its scheduled flights, cancelling fewer than any other US carrier.Source 6

  • 77.77%: Southwest on-time arrivals, 2024 — last of the five largest US carriers
  • 99.38%: Southwest flights completed — fewer cancellations than any other US carrier
  • 0.01: Percentage points between American and Southwest on punctuality

An airline that cancels less keeps more difficult flights inside its own on-time calculation, including the ones it could have removed.

Decision 2 of 5

Delta was on time 83.46% of the time. Southwest, 77.77% — and it cancelled fewer flights than anyone.

Which airline got more passengers where they were going?

Chapter 04

The airlines' position

An airline controls one side of this equation and not the other.

It cannot reliably control how long a flight takes. Weather, air traffic control, congestion at the gate and the condition of the aircraft that arrived before it all sit outside any one carrier's hands. In July 2024 Delta Air Lines cancelled roughly seven thousand flights over five days when the CrowdStrike software outage disabled its crew-tracking systems. Its annual on-time figure fell by just over a point, from 84.7% to 83.46%.Source 6 Nothing about Delta's operation had changed. A piece of software had.

Jeremy Bowen, chief executive of the aviation analytics firm Cirium, described 2024 as a difficult year for airlines, citing severe weather and the summer outage, and said the carriers that performed well deserved credit for it.Source 7

What they do control

What an airline does control is the time printed on the ticket.

Scheduled block time runs gate to gate, pushback to arrival. It is set by scheduling teams working from historical flight data, weather patterns, air traffic control behavior and seasonal shifts.Source 8 Setting it is genuine analytical work, and there is no single correct answer — a route has a distribution of outcomes, not a duration. Choosing where in that distribution to publish is a judgment.

What happened

10%

Robert Shumsky examined 219 flights across 1987 to 1991 and found that major carriers increased their scheduled gate-to-gate times by roughly ten per cent over the period. Actual gate-to-gate times did not fall to match.Source 9

On-time performance improved by around twenty per cent over the same five years.Source 10

  • +10%: Increase in scheduled gate-to-gate times, 1987–1991
  • +20%: Improvement in on-time performance over the same five years
  • 219: Flights in the Shumsky sample
Image description

Two lines over a five-year axis. The scheduled time printed on the ticket climbs from 150 to 165 minutes, roughly ten per cent. The actual flight duration stays flat at between 135 and 136 minutes.

Exhibit 3: Scheduled against actual block time, 1987–1991

Illustrative. Shumsky examined 219 flights across the period and reports an overall increase of roughly ten per cent in scheduled gate-to-gate times, with actual times not falling to match. Year-by-year values are not published, so the chart shows the shape of the change rather than plotted data.

Nothing was falsified. No flight was recorded incorrectly. Every scheduling team was doing the job it had been given, with the data it had been told to use, and each could point to a defensible reason for the number it chose.

The trade

The number that passengers could see went up. The time they spent travelling did not go down.

Chapter 05

What it cost them

The easy reading is that airlines found a free way to look better. They did not, and the costs matter because they are what makes the behavior a trade rather than a trick.

Aircraft utilization

A longer scheduled time means an aircraft completes fewer flights in a day. Aircraft are the most expensive asset an airline owns, and utilization is the number that justifies owning them.

Crew wages

Crew agreements are commonly written so that pay is calculated on the greater of scheduled or actual block time. A longer schedule therefore raises the wage bill even when the flight lands early.Source 11

Screen position

And there is a cost at the point of sale. Booking systems list shorter flights first, and travellers choose from the top of the screen. A padded schedule can push a flight down the list where fewer people see it.Source 11

Image description

Three equal segments show the costs: aircraft utilization (more time on the ground and less revenue opportunity), crew wages (more paid flight and cabin crew hours), and screen position (a longer flight drops down booking-system listings). They are set against one visible benefit: the published punctuality figure everyone sees.

Decision 3 of 5

So why keep doing it?

It costs aircraft time, wages, and screen position. Something outweighs all three.

One line. You will use these notes later, and nobody else reads them.

Chapter 06

Why it did not stop

Airline schedules are published well ahead of the flights operating. Any carrier can look up what a competitor has printed for the same route, long before a passenger books it.Source 12

That visibility turns a decision into a game. If one airline lengthens its schedule and its published figure rises, every other airline can see both the move and the result. Researchers describe what follows as an arms race in buffer time — each carrier adding a little more so as not to slip down a ranking customers are watching.Source 12

The 2024 table shows how tight that ranking is. American finished at 77.78% and Southwest at 77.77%. One hundredth of a percentage point, on a list passengers read as an order.

Decision 4 of 5

You run a competing airline

A rival has lengthened its schedules. Its published figure has risen. Yours now looks worse on a ranking your customers check. What do you do?

Chapter 07

There is a floor, and JetBlue found it

On 3 January 2025 the Department of Transportation fined JetBlue Airways $2 million. It was the first penalty the Department had ever issued for chronically delayed flights.Source 13

Airlines are not permitted to publish schedules that fail to reflect actual departure and arrival times. The Department treats a flight as chronically delayed if it operates at least ten times a month and arrives more than thirty minutes late more than half the time.Source 13

  • $2m: The first penalty ever issued for chronically delayed flights
  • 4: JetBlue routes meeting the chronically-delayed definition
  • 145+: Chronically delayed operations, June 2022 – November 2023
  • 70%: Share of the disruption the Department attributed to JetBlue
Image description

Two arrows push in the same direction on one schedule. The published on-time measure rewards a longer schedule; the enforcement rule penalises one that is too short. Both the reward and the penalty drive airlines towards the same end of the schedule.

Exhibit 4: The two thresholds

MeasureDefinitionWhat it does
On timeArrives at the gate less than 15 minutes after the scheduled arrival time.Published monthly and used in every public ranking. Rewards a schedule the airline can comfortably meet.
Chronically delayedFlown at least 10 times a month and arrives more than 30 minutes late more than half the time.Triggers enforcement. Penalizes a schedule the airline consistently misses.
Both thresholds are measured against the airline's own published schedule. One rewards lengthening it; the other penalizes leaving it too short. Sources: Bureau of Transportation Statistics; US DOT enforcement action, January 2025.

Four JetBlue routes met that definition. John F. Kennedy to Raleigh-Durham, and three out of Fort Lauderdale — to Orlando, to JFK, and to Windsor Locks in Connecticut. Between June 2022 and November 2023 those flights were chronically delayed at least 145 times, each for five consecutive months or more, with 395 delays and cancellations across them. The Department estimated JetBlue was responsible for more than seventy per cent of the disruption, and said it had warned the airline about the Raleigh-Durham route before the other three developed.Source 13

The Department

Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said the action put the industry on notice that schedules were expected to reflect reality.Source 14 Half the penalty went to the Treasury and half was set aside to compensate affected passengers. The Department said it had investigations open into other carriers.Source 13

JetBlue

JetBlue's position was that it had invested tens of millions of dollars in reducing delays and had improved through 2024, and that responsibility for reliable air travel also sits with the government, which operates the air traffic control system.Source 13

Both halves of this case are now on the table. Hold them together before you answer.

Decision 5 of 5

Which way does the regulation push?

Publishing a schedule you consistently miss is illegal. Publishing a longer one you comfortably meet is not.

Chapter 08

Back to Dallas

In 2024, 78.1% of US flights arrived on time by the Department's definition, against 78.3% the year before.Source 15

Image description

A vertical timeline from 1987 to April 2026. The January 2025 JetBlue fine, a $2 million DOT penalty for four chronically delayed routes flown between June 2022 and November 2023, is marked as the single enforcement event in the period.

Exhibit 5: Timeline

Rule-making

  1. 1987

    DOT begins requiring large airlines to report on-time performance. On time is defined as arriving at the gate less than 15 minutes after schedule.

  2. 1987–1991

    Period examined by Shumsky. Scheduled gate-to-gate times rise roughly 10%; on-time performance improves roughly 20%.

  3. 1995

    Reporting rule modified to include mechanical delays.

  4. 2000

    Air Carrier On-Time Reporting Advisory Committee formed.

  5. Nov 2002

    Final rule requires airlines to report the causes of delays and cancellations.

Enforcement and response

  1. Jun 2022 – Nov 2023

    JetBlue operates four chronically delayed routes at least 145 times.

  2. Jul 2024

    CrowdStrike outage; Delta cancels approximately 7,000 flights over five days.

  3. 2024

    US on-time arrivals 78.10%, against 78.34% in 2023.

  4. 3 Jan 2025

    First enforcement action

    DOT fines JetBlue $2 million for chronically delayed flights — the first penalty of its kind.

  5. 27 Dec 2025

    American announces the DFW restructure and a network-wide block time increase.

  6. Apr 2026

    American's thirteen-bank structure takes effect at Dallas Fort Worth.

Compiled from the sources listed below. Thirty-eight years between the rule and the first enforcement action taken under it.

Eleven months after the JetBlue fine, American Airlines announced the changes at Dallas Fort Worth. The thirteen-bank structure took effect in April 2026, and American has since reported that on-time arrivals improved shortly after the switch and that baggage performance at the hub was its strongest of the year.Source 16

Read the announcement a third time, because it is not dishonest. A longer schedule really does absorb disruption. A passenger who lands when the ticket said they would has had a better day than one who did not, and a buffer that stops a single delay cascading through an aircraft's remaining rotations is doing operational work, not only reporting work.Source 17

It is also true that the journey takes longer than it used to, and that the number the public sees went up.

Practice

Two questions before you move on

Question 1

Which part of how this was set up is doing the work here?

One sentence. Name the number that moved and the thing that did not.

In closing

Both thresholds measure a flight against a schedule the airline wrote.

Nobody has ever been penalized for writing a generous one.
